stories.title: Comedian and presenter PJ Gallagher dies aged 51
stories.summary: The stand-up comedian and actor known for Naked Camera and The Young Offenders also worked on television documentaries, features and radio, including as part of the breakfast show team on Radio Nova with presenter Jim McCabe. As well as co-creating the show, Gallagher played the newspaper swinging Jake Stevens, among other iconic characters. The hidden camera show involved Gallagher and his co-stars, such as Father Ted's Pat McDonnell and comedian Maeve Higgins, jovially accosting unsuspecting members of the public. Later, Gallagher starred in sketch show Meet Your Neighbours, in which he played all the core roles. More recently, he appeared in The Young Offenders TV series as principal Barry Walsh. He had played a drug dealer in the initial film version of the series. Also a stand up comedian, Gallagher took the stage at the Iveagh Gardens for six editions of the Vodafone Comedy Festival, as it was then known.

stories.title: DPD delivers operating profits of €28.9m, revenues rise
stories.summary:
Ireland's largest dedicated parcel delivery firm DPD last year delivered an 8.5% increase in operating profits to €28.9m. In another stellar year for the Athlone headquartered delivery firm, revenues at Interlink Ireland Ltd rose by 8% from €201.2m to €217.36m in the period to January 4, 2026. The operating profits of €28.9m last year follow operating profits of €26.6m in 2024 and on the back of strong profits over recent years, the firm paid a dividend of €11m in June of this year. The €11m dividend followed the company paying out a dividend of €70m in 2024. In only one other year, the firm has achieved higher revenues when it recorded revenues of €220m in 2022.

In their report, the directors state that turnover has continued to increase steadily from the previous period. They state that "the expectation of management is that turnover will remain consistent if not slightly increase in the following periods".

stories.title: Connolly focuses on next step in long journey to Brazil
stories.summary: Megan Connolly, the Republic of Ireland's gatekeeper at the base of midfield, has been around top-level football long enough to recognise the perils of looking too far ahead. Ireland travel to Poland tomorrow afternoon ahead of Tuesday's World Cup play-off first leg against Poland where conditions are forecast to be sub-zero. Then, they come back to Dublin for an enormous return game at Aviva Stadium the following Saturday. The mantra in the camp this week has been simple: focus on Gdansk, then worry about Lansdowne Road. It's a monumental period, but 29-year-old Connolly is staying grounded. "There's no shying away from the fact that everybody wants to be at the World Cup and for us it's massive," said the Lazio player. "It's what you dream of as a little kid and being there once, you want to continue to be at major tournaments. So there's no doubt that we know how big of an opportunity this is for us. But yeah, we're trying not to get too hyped up or too focused on all that stuff because sometimes when you put on extra pressure and get too into it, it kind of affects your performances and your preparation.

stories.title: Colin Farrell on opening hearts with The Slightest Touch
stories.summary: The documentary The Slightest Touch tells the story of epidermolysis bullosa (EB) campaigner Emma Fogarty's friendship with Colin Farrell and their countdown to the 2024 Dublin City Marathon. It's no spoiler to say that Colin Farrell ran the marathon and Emma Fogarty joined him in a modified wheelchair for the last four kilometres, each representing a decade of her life. In the process, they raised over €1m for the EB charity DEBRA Ireland. Although their achievement has been well publicised, it doesn't diminish the power of The Slightest Touch, which effortlessly moves from joy to sadness and back again under the expert stewardship of director Rachel Fleit. Below, Colin Farrell and Rachel Fleit discuss bringing Emma Fogarty's story to the screen and the heart-warming response to the film. Harry Guerin: I had thought watching the film that you two (Colin Farrell and Rachel Fleit) were friends from way, way back. I couldn't believe that you had only met during the making of it. So how quickly did that friendship click into place? Colin Farrell: You know the way sometimes you meet people and you feel even if you're separated by nationality or by 3,000 miles - she (Rachel Fleit) was born in New York, I was born in Dublin - that you feel they're your tribe? That there's an unspoken understanding that goes beyond the time you've spent [together]? Well, it was like that with her as well. It was very, very easy from [the] first [moment].

stories.title: Laura de Barra shares her tips for decorating the Christmas tree
stories.summary: Gaff Goddess, Laura de Barra, tells Oliver Callan about the 2026 festive trends and shares her advice for prolonging your fresh Christmas tree. Listen back above. Christmas comes earlier and earlier every year, it seems, and with it the quandary: which way to decorate the tree. For some households the same baubles, lights, tufts of tinsel and star go up every year, while others like to rotate a selection of decorations depending on colours and styles. With Ireland topping a new global ranking of the countries with the most fast fashion waste, many of us will be thinking of the ways we can cut down on waste this festive season. But as Laura de Barra notes, over-consumption is finding ever more ways into Christmas. Talking to Oliver about what she calls 'fast Christmas' - the onslaught of trends and novelties that pop up at Christmas - de Barra says she's spotted everything from Ozempic and Botox syringes to Claudia Winkleman-shaped baubles in stores. "It is actually a genius way for brands because the Christmas shop floor", she says, adding that brands "would pay so much money to have advertising there".

stories.title: Israeli strike kills two Doctors Without Borders staff
stories.summary: Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has said an Israeli strike killed two staff members at a clinic in Gaza, with the Israeli army labelling the pair as Hamas "terrorists". The medical humanitarian organisation said it was "devastated" by the killings and denounced "a direct hit" on the organisation. "Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military," it wrote on X. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) identified the men, who worked as security guards at the clinic, as Hamas artillery cell commander Moaz Yousef Alitsbach and Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu. 🔴 BREAKING - We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight. This is a direct hit on MSF, bringing the total number of MSF colleagues killed in Gaza to 17. Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military. We stand in solidarity with the families and loved ones of our colleagues. We call for accountability. World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus criticised the strike.

stories.title: ECB's gender gap set to widen further after Lagarde exit
stories.summary: The European Central Bank is on course to become the most male-dominated major central bank in the world when President Christine Lagarde leaves in February, a jarring outcome for an institution that has spent years promoting gender balance. The departure of Lagarde, a vocal advocate of greater female representation, and fellow board member Isabel Schnabel will leave just one woman among the ECB's 27 policymakers - a lower proportion than at Saudi Arabia's central bank. The comparison is uncomfortable for an institution that has made gender diversity a hallmark of the Lagarde era. Research suggests the consequences can extend beyond appearance, with studies linking more diverse monetary policy committees to broader debate and even different responses to inflation. "An institution whose decisions affect 350 million Europeans cannot afford to ignore half of the available talent," said Stéphanie Yon-Courtin, who sits on the European Parliament committee that oversees the ECB. "Without calling for strict parity at all costs, we are far from where we should be." A Reuters analysis of 20 major central banks found that women hold about 28% of seats on their top policymaking bodies.

stories.title: Ireland recover from slow start to fend off Wallabies
stories.summary: Ireland will head into a World Cup year in good health after they made it a clean sweep for their Nations championship November. Andy Farrell's side never quite hit the same heights as last week's win against the world champions South Africa, but after surviving an iffy opening quarter they fended off Australia 38-14 at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham. Their win confirms they finish fifth in the unofficial standings in the first Nations Championship, but the overall ranking mattered far less than the performance, in what was their 11th and final game of 2026. For 20 minutes Ireland struggled to even touch the ball as some inaccurate passing and a raft of penalties invited the Wallabies onto them, with Les Kiss's side taking a 7-0 lead after Jeremy Williams' try. It was the splash of water in the face that Ireland needed, with tries for Robbie Henshaw and Nick Timoney, along with two conversions and a penalty from Sam Prendergast nudging them 17-7 ahead at the break. Rob Baloucoune's try after half time gave them a comfortable buffer, but they had to weather a Wallaby storm for large periods, before James McNabney (below) continued his impressive fledgling Test career with two tries in the final 10 minutes to hammer home victory.

stories.title: Daniel O'Donnell among winners at Irish Post Awards
stories.summary: Daniel O'Donnell received an award for Lifetime Contribution to Country Music at the 49th Irish Post Awards in London on Thursday night. The country music singer was honoured at a gala dinner at the Grosvenor House Hotel on Park Lane in front of more than a thousand guests, who were treated to an impromptu performance by Mr O’Donnell and Fermanagh band The Tumbling Paddies. Actor Aidan Gillen, comedian Dara O’Brien, TV presenter and podcaster Vogue Williams, rugby star Brian O’Driscoll and TV personality Gloria Hunniford were among nine honourees recognised for their outstanding work as Irish people in Britain. Hosted by Ryan Tubridy and Lisa McHugh, and sponsored by the Irish Post newspaper and website, the black tie event was strongly supported by Irish firms involved in construction, development and finance in the UK. Irish Post publisher Elgin Loan paid a special tribute to Irish dancer Niamh O’Brien, the late wife of Michael Flatley, who passed away last month. Mr Loan said the Flatleys were great supporters of the Irish Post Awards, and said the event simply would not have happened in some years were it not for the strong support of the couple.

The maritime rescue service had earlier said between eight and ‌10 bodies were found on ⁠board and six people were airlifted to a hospital in serious condition. Eighty-four survivors disembarked from a separate boat at the island's La Restinga port, home to a migrant reception centre ‌and field hospital where most migrant boats reaching the island have been processed. Migrant arrivals to the Canary ⁠Islands have accelerated since October, hitting a record 2,100 people in a single day ‌on 25 November, most of them coming to El Hierro, population 11,400.

stories.title: How are Ireland's data centres affecting the electricity grid?
stories.summary: Analysis: 'No other country in the world has anywhere near as large a proportion of its electricity used by data centres as Ireland' Over the past decade, data centres have become a much larger part of Ireland's electricity demand. In 2015 they accounted for 5% of total metered electricity consumption. By 2025 that share had risen to 23%, and this is projected to increase to 31% by 2034. No other country in the world has anywhere near as large a proportion of its electricity used by data centres. This pace and scale of growth has brought new challenges for Ireland and one of the most pressing is the impact on the electricity grid. How can Ireland manage its electricity grid to deliver on climate action, support new housing, power public transport and other essential infrastructure as well as supply data centres? Electricity is generated at different locations and transported through power lines and cables before reaching homes and businesses. The electricity grid has physical limits, determined by the size of the cables, transformers and substations, as well as the need to maintain secure and reliable operation. This means that connecting a new electricity user is not simply a matter of having enough electricity generation available nationally. The network must also be capable of delivering that electricity to the right location, at the right time. Network capacity is a shared resource and a public good rather than an issue for individual projects alone. We are all connected to the grid and reliant on it. When considering connecting to the electricity grid, size matters. Data centres are part of a decades-long trend towards increasing digitalisation and represent an industrialised version of what started as computer server racks in businesses. To put the scale in perspective, a modern data centre drawing 50 MW (megawatts of power) continuously would use around nine times as much electricity as St James's Hospital (one of Ireland’s biggest hospitals) used in total energy, including electricity and fuel, in 2025.

stories.title: Player ratings: Ulster men to the fore in Aussie crushing
stories.summary: Ireland ended their 2026 year with an emphatic 38-14 win over Australia in Twickenham's opening night screening of the Nations Championship finals weekend. Andy Farrell's men crossed five times on a cold night in London, and here is how we rated them. Started with two early knock-ons on a much tougher night in the aerial game for the 51-times capped fullback. Coughed up an inconsequential, and harsh, penalty for a tackle on the air; before finishing the game on the wing. Returning to the stage where he lit up the Six Nations, the Ulster winger always threatened, even if James Ramm did well to limit his explosiveness. Very nearly had a stellar solo try before the break before getting in on the act with Ireland’s third to take him to nine tries in his last ten games. Replaced due to a knock before the hour after another top performance.

stories.title: Can your aching joints really predict the weather?
stories.summary: Analysis: While the phenomenon remains scientifically contentious, research suggests those with joint conditions are more attuned to environmental changes For centuries, people have claimed that their aching joints can predict changes in the weather, often reporting increased discomfort before rain or cold fronts. Given the scale and duration, there is a sense of legitimacy to these anecdotes, but this phenomenon remains scientifically contentious. From shifts in barometric pressure to temperature fluctuations, many theories attempt to explain how environmental factors might influence joint pain. But is there an anatomical basis for this claim, or is it simply an enduring weather-related myth? Are our joints any more reliable than the weather forecast? From Premier Health, what is the relationship between weather and joint pain? At the heart of this debate lies barometric pressure, also known as atmospheric pressure – the force exerted by air molecules in the Earth's atmosphere. While invisible, air has mass, and the "weight" pressing down on us fluctuates with altitude and weather systems. Higher barometric pressure often signals fair-weather conditions with clear skies and calm winds, whereas lower pressure typically precedes unsettled weather, such as cloudy skies, precipitation and humidity. Moveable joints are intricate structures cushioned by synovial fluid, the viscous liquid that lubricates joints, and encased in capsules rich in nerve endings. In healthy joints, these components should allow smooth, pain-free movement. However, when joints are compromised by cartilage damage (as in osteoarthritis) or inflammation (as in rheumatoid arthritis), even subtle changes in the environment may be acutely felt.

stories.title: The exiled Russian charity helping men avoid conscription
stories.summary: Leaked figures published by independent Russian media outlets earlier this week show that more than 490,000 Russian soldiers were killed in Ukraine between February 2022, when Moscow launched its full-scale invasion, and the end of September 2026. Two hacking collectives, Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow, a pro-Ukrainian group, hacked into the databases of Rosstat, Russia's Federal State Statistics Service, to extract 11 million death certificates. The groups then shared the data sets in early November with independent Russian media outlets, iStories, Meduza and Mediazona, as well as BBC Russian. Both Meduza and Mediazona estimate that the true death toll may be closer to 720,000 Russian soldiers when missing combatants and deaths that have not yet been registered are included. Such a staggering death toll is a sobering indictment of Russian President Vladimir Putin's decision to invade Ukraine. Going by the 490,000 figure, iStories calculated that one in 17 deaths of Russian citizens since 2022 have been due to the war.
stories.rssSummary: Since 2009, School of the Conscript, a Russian NGO, has offered legal advice to thousands of young Russians who want to avoid compulsory military service. The organisation's director told RTÉ News how Moscow's invasion of Ukraine changed the way the group works.

stories.title: Farrell: 'We dug in deep and we fought and fought'
stories.summary: Andy Farrell believes his side "dug in" when it was needed as they completed a clean sweep for their Nations Championship November with a 38-14 win against Australia. Ireland recovered from a sloppy opening quarter to score five converted tries against the Wallabies, with James McNabney crossing the line twice in another eye-catching cameo, while Sam Prendergast impressed with six out of six off the tee for a 13-point haul. Ireland could hardly touch the ball for the opening 20 minutes of the game, but came alive after falling behind, and turned their only three entries to the 22 in the opening half into two tries and a penalty, for a 17-7 lead. "I think [it was] pretty similar to last week really," Farrell (below) said at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham. "I mean, last week's game or performance obviously it gets highlighted a little bit more because of the nature of the opposition that you're playing against, being the world's best South Africa, but it was a stop-start game where things weren't really going our way all the time as well. "And that was very similar [today] in the sense that we had no field position, no ball, a lot down to Australia, but most of it was down to ourselves as well – giving penalties away and not winning the ball that we wanted to win.

stories.title: US military says it fired on ship violating Iran blockade
stories.summary: The United States military has announced that it disabled a Palau-flagged ship violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports. Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US forces in the Middle East, said an American aircraft had fired "precision munitions" on Thursday into the Pacific Archer's stern after it attempted to run the blockade. "The ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," the statement said, noting the incident occurred in the Gulf of Oman. The Pacific Archer had left Bandar Abbas, an Iranian port on the Strait of Hormuz, the statement said. CENTCOM said it "continues to strictly enforce the blockade", which has seen six ships disabled and 158 others redirected. CENTCOM disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Nov. 26, after the crew attempted to run the U.S. naval blockade, despite multiple warnings, following departure from Bandar Abbas. A U.S. military aircraft launched precision munitions that struck the stern of Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer. The ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed. stories.title: Azaz has no regrets over Saints goal celebration
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland international Finn Azaz insisted he had not regrets about his goal celebration after he scored the second Southampton's 2-0 victory over Middlesbrough. Azaz, who joined Saints from Boro in the summer of 2025 after two successful seasons at the Riverside, scored in in the 79th minute before inciting a fracas. The forward picked up on an Aidan Morris slip-up to coolly place it into the bottom corner – and then ran the length of the St Mary's pitch to celebrate in front of the travelling fans, making crying motions as he ran. stories.title: Storing wind: Why are we losing renewable energy?
stories.summary: There is no question about the sense of urgency surrounding Ireland's energy situation. The crises driven by the wars in Iran and Ukraine highlighted the country's dependency on fossil fuels. Ireland's electricity prices were the highest in Europe in the first six months of this year, at €0.38 per kWh, according to Eurostat. Using renewable sources could potentially lower electricity costs or at least make them less exposed to global volatility. Yet, so far Ireland has remained below the EU average in its share of renewables in electricity consumption: around 42% in 2025. Countries like Austria (90%), Denmark (89%), and Portugal (65%) among the leaders (the latter two are also quite windy, though that's not the only reason for their progress).

stories.title: St Eunan's objection to Ulster Club SFC loss unsuccessful
stories.summary: St Eunan's objection to their controversial defeat to Scotstown in the Ulster Club SFC semi-final has been unsuccessful. St Eunan's club officials met with Ulster GAA on Friday night to discuss their provincial semi-final exit. The Letterkenny club sought clarification after a late free from Scotstown's Kieran Hughes in extra-time appeared to go wide. Both umpires were unsure of whether Hughes' fee went over the bar or not. Referee Kieran Eannetta consulted with them before awarding the score. The Monaghan men won a subsequent penalty shootout to march into a final clash against Crossmaglen on 6 December. St Eunan's manager Kieran Donnelly said afterwards that the Donegal champions had been let down by officials, while on Monday evening the club released a statement saying they were escalating the matter. Meanwhile Granemore's appeal to the Disputes Resolution Authority has also proven unsuccessful.

stories.title: Bikes, trains, or both? Future of Sligo Greenway elusive
stories.summary: Two significant meetings on the future of the Western Rail Corridor took place this week - the first in Leinster House and the second in a Sligo hotel, where local TDs were elected in 2024. On Thursday night, more than 300 people attended the launch of a campaign seeking to reinstate the Sligo to Galway railway, which closed to passenger services in 1963. A day earlier, a delegation from the Sligo Greenway Cooperative, supported by their three local Government TDs, held a meeting with the Taoiseach in Leinster House. The Government supports a planned 35km Sligo Greenway, along the disused rail corridor between Collooney and Bellaghy, without precluding future rail. Rail campaigners are seeking the preservation of that rail alignment for a full reinstatement of passenger and freight train services between Galway and Sligo. The launch of the rail campaign follows a decision by Irish Rail to lease the disused rail alignment between Collooney and Bellaghy to Sligo County Council for a 35km greenway.

stories.title: Manning and Azaz score as Saints sink Middlesbrough
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland duo Ryan Manning and Finn Azaz gave Southampton a 2-0 victory over Middlesbrough and the Spygate bragging rights. Full-back Manning opened the scoring with a tidy finish before Azaz capitalised on a defensive mistake to slide in – before running the length of St Mary's to celebrate in front of his former fans. It allowed Saints to move to a 19th home match without defeat and move within four points of Boro at the summit. This was the first meeting between Southampton and Middlesbrough since the Spygate scandal – where Saints sent a member of staff to watch Boro train before the play-offs last season. The South Coast side – who also illicitly viewed Ipswich and Oxford sessions – were kicked out of the play-offs and docked four points for this season. Boro were reinstated in their place, but lost to Hull at Wembley and missed out on Premier League promotion.

stories.title: Man charged with murder of Qayyum Balogun in Dublin
stories.summary: A man has appeared in court charged with the murder of 21-year-old student Qayyum Balogun in Dublin last June. Mr Balogun died after he was pursued and stabbed in an unprovoked attack during a night out in Dublin city centre. Joshua Brodericks, 26, with an address at Gleann Dara, Rahoon in Galway was charged with his murder and remanded in custody for a week. Mr Balogun was found fatally injured on Clarendon Street following a late-night rap concert at Bewley's on Grafton Street almost six months ago. The Maynooth computer science student, originally from Nigeria and living in Co Louth, was found in the early hours of 1 June and was treated by emergency services at the scene before being rushed to St James's Hospital, where he was later pronounced dead. Joshua Brodericks, 26, with an address at Gleann Dara, Rahoon, Galway, had been granted conditional bail on 5 June after he was charged with assault causing harm to 24-year-old Oreoluwa Amosu, who was a friend of the deceased, at Grafton Street.

stories.title: Rooney inquest hears evidence on disinformation campaign
stories.summary: The inquest into the death of Private Seán Rooney has heard evidence around "assumptions being made" that the attack on his vehicle was connected to a disinformation campaign and a direct response to UNIFIL being allowed to act independently in Lebanon. Pte Rooney, 24, from Newtowncunningham, Co Donegal, suffered fatal gunshot wounds in an attack which took place near the Lebanese village of Aaqbiyeh on 14 December 2022 after a two-vehicle military convoy became separated. The deceased, who was attached to the 27th Infantry Battalion at Aiken Barracks in Dundalk, Co Louth, was driving a UN-marked vehicle which was fired on by armed militia linked to Hezbollah while they were trying to escape from a group of locals who had surrounded their jeep in Aaqbiyeh. The first witness this morning, an intelligence specialist, was granted anonymity, as he told the court about the circumstances leading up to and around the incident. His deposition read out in the court described "the very high-pressure environment" in the Tactical Operations Centre (TOC) at Camp Shamrock on the night Pte Rooney's vehicle came under attack. He explained how staff in the TOC tried to get the exact coordinates of the vehicles in the convoy and how they found out the two vehicles had become separated.

stories.title: Driver who was on phone when lorry struck woman is jailed
stories.summary: A lorry driver who was on the phone when he struck a 72-year-old woman on Main Street in Charleville, Co Cork, causing her death, has been jailed for nine months. Margaret Lyons of Ardmore, Charleville and late of Garristown, Co Dublin, died on 15 May 2023. The mother-of-five and grandmother-of-six was pronounced dead at the scene. Cork Circuit Criminal Court heard that Damien Mulvey of Avondale, Knockbarry, Buttevant, Co Cork, was driving at a speed of 11km/h when he collided with the pensioner. Garda Sean Lynam said that CCTV footage from the scene showed he was holding what looked to be a mobile phone at the time of the offence. He had insisted he was on Bluetooth and not physically holding a phone when the collision occurred.

stories.title: Thompson cleared of assault, threats to kill officer
stories.summary: A man described in court as a major player in the Kinahan organised crime group has been cleared of assaulting and threatening to kill a prison officer four years ago. Frederick Thompson, 45, was on trial at Tullamore Circuit Court having denied committing the offences at Portlaoise Prison where he is serving a life sentence. Thompson had been accused of threatening to kill or cause serious harm to TJ Pender, an assistant chief officer at the prison, on 18 May 2022. The prisoner had been accused of committing the same offence again on 17 November 2022, along with an additional charge of assaulting Mr Pender, causing him harm. While the jury heard Thompson was serving a life sentence for murder and was being held in Ireland's high security prison, Judge Ronan Munro ruled that he could not be referred to as a major player in the Kinahan organised crime group. The jury heard Mr Pender give evidence that in his role as assistant chief officer at Portlaoise Prison he was in charge of a block where Thompson was housed.

stories.title: Ward desperate to take Ireland 'project' to next level
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland boss Carla Ward admitted she has batted away other offers to stick with the Girls in Green and help them break more barriers ahead of their World Cup play-off against Poland. Ireland are in Gdansk for the first leg on Tuesday, before the Poles come to Aviva Stadium the following Saturday. It's a massive week, with confirmation of Ward's contract renewal on Monday night helping to keep the camp calm and focused. It was, the 41-year-old Englishwoman insists, never in doubt. "I'm delighted to get that done and dusted and now the full focus can be on solely the football," she said at FAI HQ on Friday. "The reaction (from the players) has been good. I've had a number of conversations with players and obviously seen some of the interviews that have been done and probably recognised that maybe it was important for them. It wasn't something that I thought about." Asked if there'd been other clubs or countries circling prior to Ward penning the deal, she replied: "There's been interest, yes, but I'm not interested. I think I've been really clear for a long time. I love this job. I think when you look at my career I'm not someone to jump ship.

Tanzania provided a stern test in the final group game, but a well-managed second half was a great sign for head coach John Cotter and his staff as they look to keep building. Ireland can be very happy with their group stage performances and head confidently into the round of 32. Cotter's charges kept hold of the ball early on and this game burst into action early. In the sixth minute, Ryan Sheridan got on the end of a loose ball in Tanzania's half. He played a quick pass to Murphy who, rifled the ball into the bottom corner from the edge of the box.

stories.title: Spanish PM in bid to beat the right ahead of key poll
stories.summary: Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez made a final push to overcome the odds today - the last day of campaigning for an election this weekend expected to deliver a victory for conservatives and the far right. The outcome of Sunday's vote will be closely watched as Europe opens an electoral cycle over the next 12 months that could reshape the balance of power within the European Union. Mr Sanchez has enhanced his global profile in recent years as one of the world's most prominent leftist leaders but a polarising status at home puts his eight-year tenure in peril. Polls have consistently put him behind the main right-wing Popular Party (PP), which is predicted to win the most seats in another hung parliament. It could therefore rely on far-right, anti-immigration Vox, Spain's third-largest political force, which could double its seats and already governs several regions with the PP. Such a coalition would be a first since Spain's transition to democracy after General Francisco Franco's fascist-backed dictatorship from 1939 to 1975.
